profiles.meeting_scenario: At a university-affiliated medical innovation program, a rehabilitation physician and the engineering commercialization lead are holding a brainstorming meeting to shape a new student-led project around a portable hand-function rehabilitation device for stroke survivors. The context is that the program wants a concept suitable for an interdisciplinary MEng 'virtual company' team that can both address a real clinical need and plausibly advance toward commercialization over the next academic year. Their agenda is to generate and loosely screen a few concept directions, discuss what a first pilot and early user feedback might look like, and frame the opportunity in a way that will attract both engineering and business students. The expected outcome is a shortlist of 2-3 concept directions plus a shared-sounding plan for what kind of early testing, target users, and cost framing the student team should use.

members.name: Dr. Elena Park
members.role: Associate Professor of Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation; clinical advisor for stroke rehab innovation
members.expertise: Inpatient stroke rehabilitation, therapy workflow design, clinician-led unmet-needs identification, early device usability in rehabilitation settings
members.background: Dr. Park runs the inpatient stroke service at a large teaching hospital and has mentored several senior capstone teams that built clinician-facing rehab tools and therapy aids for use inside the hospital.
members.private_state: She wants the project to solve a concrete problem her therapists face on the rehab floor and to produce something simple enough to be tested quickly with minimal disruption or regulatory friction; she is also wary of student teams overpromising home-use features before proving clinical usefulness in supervised settings.
hidden_assumptions: When people say a device can be 'piloted in clinic,' they usually mean a small therapist-supervised usability tryout embedded in existing rehab sessions rather than a formal deployment meant to demonstrate market traction.
An 'affordable' rehab device is one a hospital therapy department could justify buying from a discretionary equipment budget, even if the build cost is still relatively high at prototype volumes.
References to 'our stroke population' naturally point to the inpatients on the rehab floor, because that is where she sees the need most vividly and where clinician access is easiest.
Early user feedback can be gathered through therapist-mediated interactions during ordinary treatment sessions, with students observing indirectly rather than leading patient-facing interviews.

members.name: Aaron Feld
members.role: Director of Design and Commercialization Programs; biomedical engineer and venture mentor
members.expertise: Medical device product strategy, student venture formation, manufacturability, customer discovery, university translational project design
members.background: Aaron manages the master's-level innovation-commercialization program where engineering, life sciences, and business students work as a 'virtual company' to move medical device concepts from prototype toward licensing or startup formation.
members.private_state: He wants a project that can survive beyond a class prototype by fitting a credible commercialization path, ideally with repeat-use data and a cost story that makes sense outside a single academic hospital; he is also trying to keep the concept attractive to business students looking for a scalable market.
hidden_assumptions: A 'clinic pilot' implies a limited real-world deployment that generates structured usage evidence and workflow learnings relevant to investors, partners, or future regulatory planning.
An 'affordable' device should have unit economics that could work at early manufacturing scale for outpatient clinics or eventual home use, not just for a one-off hospital purchase.
When someone mentions 'the stroke population,' the commercially relevant default is mild-to-moderate outpatient survivors who can use a device repeatedly over weeks.
Early user feedback in this program normally means direct student-led interviews or testing sessions using the innovation program's standard customer-discovery process.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both say the student team should aim for 'a clinic pilot' by spring.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a small therapist-supervised usability tryout with a handful of patients during ordinary inpatient rehab sessions, mainly to see whether the concept is practical and safe to handle.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means a more structured limited deployment that yields repeat-use evidence, workflow observations, and a commercialization-ready story about adoption in a real care setting.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In academic medical innovation settings, 'pilot' is a familiar umbrella term that comfortably covers both informal usability work and more product-oriented field testing, so each hears the phrase as confirming alignment rather than as something needing unpacking.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree the concept should be 'affordable' or 'low-cost' to improve adoption.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 evaluates affordability at the department-purchase level: if a rehab unit can buy one or two devices for roughly a few thousand dollars, the concept is affordable enough for early clinical use.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 evaluates affordability at the scalable product level: the concept should plausibly reach roughly sub-$300 cost of goods and a viable price point for outpatient clinics or home users.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are positively oriented toward cost-conscious design, and in brainstorming meetings 'affordable' sounds like a shared value rather than a threshold with embedded assumptions about buyer, volume, and commercialization stage.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They repeatedly discuss designing for 'our stroke population' and mention getting feedback from that group.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is picturing inpatients on the hospital's stroke rehab floor, including people early after stroke with substantial impairment and short daily therapy windows.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is picturing ambulatory outpatient stroke survivors from the affiliated neuro-recovery clinic, especially those with mild-to-moderate hand deficits who can use a device repeatedly over time.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The same institution serves both groups under a shared stroke-rehab umbrella, and both participants routinely collaborate across programs, so the phrase sounds specific enough even though each is anchoring to a different patient cohort.

misalignment_points.topic: How early user feedback will be obtained
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree the team can 'get user feedback next month through the program.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes therapists will introduce rough concepts during scheduled treatment sessions and relay reactions, with students mainly observing or debriefing staff afterward.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes students will directly conduct short customer-discovery interviews and hands-on mockup sessions with patients using the program's usual innovation-study templates.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both institutions already have established pathways for interacting with patients, and the phrase 'through the program' sounds like a settled logistical detail rather than a place where methods, permissions, and participant roles might differ.

turns.inner_thought: What I keep seeing on the inpatient rehab floor is that patients early after stroke get only limited hand practice outside the therapist-guided moments, and therapists need something very simple they can fold into existing sessions without creating safety or setup burdens. If this student team stays grounded in that immediate clinical gap, we can actually try something quickly with our inpatients.
turns.utterance: One recurring problem on the stroke service is that people just don't get enough meaningful hand practice between the therapist-guided tasks. I think there could be a nice student project around a portable hand-function rehab device if we keep it focused on a real rehab-floor need.

turns.inner_thought: This could be strong if we frame it as a product platform rather than a one-off therapy gadget. Portable and affordable are attractive for the MEng teams, and business students will engage if they can see a path beyond one hospital. I need something that can eventually make sense for broader outpatient or even home use, not just a bespoke inpatient tool.
turns.utterance: I agree, that sounds promising. Portable hand rehab is a space where there may be room for something affordable and practical, and if we frame it well, it fits nicely with how our MEng teams move concepts toward commercialization.

turns.inner_thought: For our stroke population, I am thinking about the inpatients my therapists see every day—people with limited time, variable attention, and often pretty significant weakness. The concept has to be therapist-friendly, quick to set up, and tolerant of a busy rehab schedule. If it needs long orientation or independent use, it will fail immediately on the unit.
turns.utterance: Yes, and I think it should really work for our stroke population on the rehab side. Whatever the team explores has to be straightforward enough that therapists can set it up quickly during normal sessions.

turns.inner_thought: When she says our stroke population, I'm hearing the ambulatory neuro-recovery patients who come back repeatedly and could use a device over weeks. That's great, because repeated use would let the team learn about engagement, adherence, and what actually drives adoption. If they can see use across multiple visits, that sets up a much stronger pilot story later.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. If our stroke population can keep using something over multiple visits, the team could learn a lot from repeated use patterns and what keeps people engaged.

turns.inner_thought: By spring, I'd like the students to have something robust enough that therapists can handle it safely in ordinary inpatient sessions with a handful of patients. I am not looking for a formal deployment—just a modest clinic pilot to see whether the idea is usable, practical, and worth refining. Anything more ambitious will bog down the team and create unnecessary friction.
turns.utterance: I think we should aim for a clinic pilot by spring. For me, the first version only needs to be robust enough that therapists can try it with a small set of patients and we can see whether it works in practice.

turns.inner_thought: A spring clinic pilot is exactly the right milestone if it gives us something more than bench validation. Ideally the team can observe workflow in a real setting, gather some structured usage evidence, and maybe see early repeat-use signals that support a commercialization narrative. That would make it much easier to recruit a strong cross-functional team and pitch the opportunity.
turns.utterance: A spring clinic pilot feels like the right target. It would be especially valuable if the team can also capture workflow observations and some repeat-use signals so the product story gets stronger as they go.

turns.inner_thought: I want affordability in the sense that a therapy department could plausibly buy one or two units without a long capital process. It doesn't need consumer-scale pricing right now; it just has to be within reach for a hospital rehab service if it proves useful. If students chase flashy complexity, they'll lose the chance to get something adopted clinically.
turns.utterance: And I would really love for it to be genuinely affordable. If a therapy department can't realistically adopt it without waiting on a major capital request, that becomes a problem pretty quickly.

turns.inner_thought: Good—affordable is exactly the right framing, but I need the students thinking about scalable unit economics from the beginning. If the mechanism, materials, and assembly only work as an expensive prototype, business students will lose interest. I want them to choose a concept that could eventually have credible margins in outpatient clinics or home channels.
turns.utterance: Absolutely. Affordability is exactly the right design constraint, and we should steer the students toward mechanisms and materials that could make the unit economics work beyond a one-off prototype.

turns.inner_thought: We should be able to get user feedback next month through the program by having my therapists surface a few rough concepts during treatment and tell the students what patients responded to. I do not want students directly leading patient interactions on the floor before the concept is mature; therapist-mediated feedback will be faster and less disruptive.
turns.utterance: We should be able to get user feedback next month through the program. Once the students have even simple mockups, my therapists can usually surface reactions pretty quickly.

turns.inner_thought: Perfect. Early user feedback next month means the students can start direct customer-discovery interviews and mockup sessions right away using our standard process. That will help them refine the need statement, narrow the use case, and build an initial business case with actual user input rather than just faculty opinion.
turns.utterance: That would be perfect timing. Early user feedback next month would give the team a strong start on customer discovery and help sharpen the initial business case.

turns.inner_thought: Feature-wise, I want the team thinking about what matters in short inpatient therapy blocks: one-handed donning, quick cleaning between users, obvious visual cues, and minimal fiddling for staff. If they solve those basics, therapists may actually try it during sessions and we can learn something useful in the clinic pilot.
turns.utterance: In terms of features, I'd push them toward very practical things: one-handed donning, quick cleaning, and visual cues that make it easy for therapists to integrate the device into short treatment blocks. If it adds complexity, it won't last long in rehab.

turns.inner_thought: This is a good project frame: portable hand rehab for the stroke population, affordable, with user feedback next month and a clinic pilot by spring. I can already see how to position it to engineering and business students as a clinically grounded concept with a credible path toward broader adoption and eventual venture or licensing potential.
turns.utterance: Great. So it sounds like the team should explore a portable hand-rehab concept for the stroke population, keep affordability front and center, get user feedback next month through the program, and work toward a clinic pilot by spring. That feels like a project both the engineering and business students can get excited about.
